name: Extracting Adverse Events with Language Models
blurb: How well LLMs pull adverse events from clinical text.
title: Extracting Adverse Events with Language Models
answer: Large language models can extract adverse events and other structured data from clinical notes and reports. A 2025 study reported human level accuracy, about 90 percent exact match, from a fine tuned open model, though at substantial computing cost, and accuracy varies with how events are described.

reading.body:
A fine tuned open model reached about 90 percent exact match extracting structured clinical data, but at substantial computing cost.

The pattern is that extraction quality now depends less on the model's general language ability than on tuning it to the specific task. A LoRA fine tuned Llama 3.1 model hit human level accuracy on one benchmark, and a review found language models outperform earlier NLP on clinical information extraction including adverse event detection. That is a real capability shift for pharmacovigilance, where case narratives arrive as free text and someone has to turn them into structured fields.

Two limits matter more than the headline number. Accuracy varies with how events are described, so performance on a published benchmark does not transfer unchanged to a different set of case narratives or languages. And the gain comes at higher computational cost than the earlier NLP it replaces, which ties the economics of safety case processing to the same compute and power constraints that govern the rest of AI.

The data covers one benchmark result and one review. It does not say how many notes were tested, which languages, which event types, or what the computing cost was in absolute terms. It also does not establish that any of this is validated for regulatory submission.

sections.body: Validate extraction on your own case narratives and languages before relying on it; accuracy on published benchmarks rarely transfers unchanged.
